An AI vendor can be sued directly for employment discrimination, as the employer's agent. The holding is two years old.

In Mobley v. Workday, the Northern District of California held that a vendor whose tools perform a traditional hiring function can plausibly be an agent of the employer, and so can face direct liability under Title VII, the ADA and the ADEA. A pleading-stage ruling, but one that has held for two years and now anchors a nationwide collective.

The scale is what makes it matter. A nationwide ADEA collective was conditionally certified in May 2025. Filings reference roughly 1.1 billion job applications processed through the platform in the covered period. In March 2026 the court held the ADEA reaches applicants, not only employees.

Three things follow for anyone buying or selling HR technology.

The vendor's liability does not reduce the employer's. Agency adds a defendant, it does not substitute one.

Indemnification language drafted for a data breach does not obviously cover a discrimination collective, and most of it was written before this theory existed.

And discovery reaches the model. How far into the algorithm plaintiffs get is one of the open questions in the case.

My read: the useful question in a vendor review is no longer whether the model is fair. It is who the agent is, and what you agreed to when you signed.

The law is behind. The evidence isn't.

Does your HR technology contract say what happens if the vendor is named?

The Most Underrated Business KPI: Hire-to-Productivity lifecycle.

We spend millions optimizing customer funnels and deploying AI copilots to save minutes off internal workflows.

Yet the most critical pipeline in business remains trapped in a legacy bottleneck:

The Hire-to-Productivity lifecycle.

In far too many enterprises, the journey looks like this: Sourcing → Multi-round panels → Approvals → Offer → Vetting → Relocation/Compliance → Day 1 → Access requests → Orientation→ Trainings → Orientation

When will these 2 become part of journey : Expected Productivity Timelines( Realistic ) → Value Delivered

Total elapsed time: 5 to 6 months.
Somehow, leadership still shrugs and calls this "standard."
It isn't standard. It is unmonitored operational drag.

The hidden cost of that delay:
Slipped roadmap delivery: Existing teams absorb burnout-level workloads to bridge capacity gaps.
Capital leakage: High-rate contractor spend spikes while recruitment overhead doubles from candidate drop-off.
Eroded employer brand: Sluggish hiring signals organizational paralysis before a candidate even joins.
And the friction doesn't end at contract signing.
If new hires spend their first month waiting for system access and chasing tribal knowledge, you are paying payroll on idle capacity.
True digital transformation isn't about using AI to schedule interviews or generate offer letters. It's about engineering the entire lifecycle around one metric: Time-to-Productivity.

Hiring is not an isolated HR chore- it is an engine of operational throughput. Onboarding is not an administrative checkpoint- it is the first stage of delivery.

Before automating a fragmented hiring cycle, we need to ask the harder question: Why does the pipeline require this many handoffs and gatekeepers in the first place?
Automating a broken workflow only produces delays faster.
Is a 6-month ramp ever genuinely justified, or have we simply normalized organizational inertia?

What does the IT market look like when you’re not actually inside development?

I have a rather strange point of view.

I'm not a developer, CTO, or architect. But every day I talk to companies that need technology and specialists, and to people who offer these technologies and expertise.
And over the years, I've noticed several patterns that are quite interesting to observe from the outside.

For example, how there is a rush around a certain technology or specialist.
Vendors, integrators and technology partners notice the demand and start hiring those specialists so they can respond to new client requests quickly.
It takes 2-3 months.
And then demand abruptly returns to normal levels.
Suddenly, several companies have expensive specialists sitting on the bench – specialists they hired because “everyone is looking for them right now.”
It turns out to be a rather paradoxical situation: the market is no longer experiencing a shortage of specialists, whom everyone was desperately looking for until recently.

Therefore, it’s hard to see today’s demand as a forecast of what will be in demand in a few months – just as it’s hard to take “which IT specialists will be most in demand in the next 2–6 months?” posts too seriously, AI/LLM/NLP engineers aside 😁

Another thing I find interesting is how differently people inside the same company can describe their approach to external vendors.
Sometimes you hear:
“We don’t work with external vendors. Everything is in-house.”
And later you discover that the company actually works with several external partners.
I don’t necessarily see this as someone being dishonest because “We don’t work with vendors” can mean many different things:
Maybe they don’t work with your type of vendor.
Maybe they don’t have a need right now.
Maybe they’re simply not the person responsible for this area.

And sometimes two people from the same company can give you completely different answers.
One person says:
“No, this isn’t something our company is interested in.”
Another says:
"What kind of expertise can you offer? Let's have a call."
And a few months later, this conversation turns into the first contract.

That's probably why one of the most interesting parts of my job is the opportunity to see the market not through one specific project or one company, but through many parallel conversations.

You begin to notice not only what companies are looking for now, but also how quickly demand is changing, which technologies are becoming "hot," how companies actually use external expertise, and how subjective even a very confident "we don't need this."

Perhaps this is one of the most unusual points of view of the IT market – to be located between those who are looking for expertise and those who are trying to offer it.

💡 A Good Business Analyst Doesn’t Just Gather Requirements — They Ask the Right QuestionsOne thing I’ve learned throughout my journey as a Business Analyst is that requirements gathering is not simply about documenting what stakeholders ask for.It’s about understanding why they need it.When a stakeholder says, “We need this feature,” I like to dig deeper:→ What business problem are we trying to solve?→ Who is affected by the current process?→ What does the process look like today?→ Where are the actual gaps or pain points?→ What data or systems are involved?→ What would success look like after implementation?Sometimes the original request is only a symptom of a much larger business problem.That’s where techniques such as stakeholder interviews, gap analysis, AS-IS/TO-BE process mapping, data analysis, user stories, acceptance criteria, and UAT become valuable.And with AI becoming part of more business solutions, I believe this mindset is even more important.Whether the solution involves traditional application development, process automation, data analytics, or Generative AI, technology should ultimately solve a real business problem and create measurable value.After around 9 years working across healthcare, banking, financial services, and insurance, this remains one of the principles I value most:Don’t start with the solution. UNBOUND debrief: Scott Thomas highlights ✨

Nobody left Scott Thomas' UNBOUND session with photos of his slides. That was the point.

Instead, every attendee walked out with three pages built on their own work: a task sort, a handoff design, and a hiring charter for an AI agent.

Scott's premise: there's a trust gap in AI, and it belongs to the companies deploying it.

→ 81% of professionals trust agentic AI with customer data. Only 36% of customers agree.

→ Customers don't have a relationship with a frontier model. They have a relationship with your support chat. Your bot is the only AI most people ever actually meet.

🗞️ The good news: trust flips after a good experience.

74% of consumers were satisfied with their last AI interaction, and over 90% when it solved the problem the first time.

The gap closes on outcomes, not tone.

The three rules Scott walked the room through:
1. Sort the work, not the org chart. Every task is Keep Human, Handshake, or Automate. IKEA got this right: its bot took 47% of routine inquiries, and 8,500 agents were retrained as design advisers instead of cut.

2. Design the handoff, not the bot. 57% of consumers would stop using a company's AI if they couldn't reach a human. Only 14% of businesses make that easy.

3. Hire the agent, don't install it. Job description, scorecard, named manager, escalation contract, last day. It's how we run June, our AI agent, who took a live call in front of the room.

⚠️ And one warning worth repeating: if your headline metric is deflection, you've built an AI that's rewarded for hanging up on people. Measure resolution.

Thank you to everyone who rolled up their sleeves in the room, and to the UNBOUND team for having us.

If you attended, share your handoff design in the comments. We'd love to see what you built.
